title: What are the rules for `this()` and `super()` calls in constructors — each must be the FIRST statement so you can use at most one per constructor, `super()` is implicitly inserted if you write neither, and constructor chaining via `this(...)` delegates to another constructor in the same class — and what happens if the superclass has no no-arg constructor (compile error unless you explicitly call `super(args)`)?
shortTitle: What are the constructor chaining rules?

s1_definition.profdef: Within a constructor, `this(...)` delegates to another constructor of the same class and `super(...)` invokes a constructor of the direct superclass. Whichever you use must be the very first statement, so a constructor can contain at most one of them and never both, and no executable code may precede it. If you write neither, the compiler implicitly inserts a no-argument `super()` as the first statement. Consequently, if the superclass declares no accessible no-argument constructor, the implicit `super()` cannot be satisfied and the code fails to compile unless the subclass constructor explicitly calls an available `super(args)` first.
s1_definition.analogy: Opening any account at National Bank of India has a strict order: the base customer record must be fully created before the specialized account details are added. `super(...)` is the step that creates the base customer record at the parent branch, and it must happen first, before anything else. `this(...)` is like a shortcut form that says "process me exactly like this other application form I already filled," routing all the real work through one master form. If the base customer record requires mandatory details and there is no "blank default" version of it, you cannot skip supplying those details; you must explicitly provide them up front, or the bank refuses to open the account at all.
s1_definition.oneliner: `this(...)` or `super(...)` must be the first statement, you get at most one, `super()` is inserted automatically if you write neither, and a parent with no no-arg constructor forces you to call `super(args)` explicitly.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Within a constructor, `this(...)` delegates to another constructor of the same class and `super(...)` invokes a constructor of the direct superclass. Whichever you use must be the very first statement, so a constructor can contain at most one of them and never both, and no executable code may precede it. If you write neither, the compiler implicitly inserts a no-argument `super()` as the first statement. Consequently, if the superclass declares no accessible no-argument constructor, the implicit `super()` cannot be satisfied and the code fails to compile unless the subclass constructor explicitly calls an available `super(args)` first.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Opening any account at National Bank of India has a strict order: the base customer record must be fully created before the specialized account details are added. `super(...)` is the step that creates the base customer record at the parent branch, and it must happen first, before anything else. `this(...)` is like a shortcut form that says "process me exactly like this other application form I already filled," routing all the real work through one master form. If the base customer record requires mandatory details and there is no "blank default" version of it, you cannot skip supplying those details; you must explicitly provide them up front, or the bank refuses to open the account at all.

**One line to remember:** `this(...)` or `super(...)` must be the first statement, you get at most one, `super()` is inserted automatically if you write neither, and a parent with no no-arg constructor forces you to call `super(args)` explicitly.

sections.s2_technical:
The language guarantees that an object is built from the top of its inheritance hierarchy downward: the superclass part is fully initialized before any subclass constructor body runs. To enforce this, the first statement of every constructor must be a call to either another constructor of the same class using `this(...)`, or a constructor of the direct superclass using `super(...)`. Because both compete for that single first slot, a constructor can contain at most one of them, and you can never write both in the same constructor.

If you write neither call, the compiler silently inserts a no-argument `super()` as the first statement for you. This is why a class with no explicit constructor still correctly initializes its parent, because the compiler-generated default constructor contains that implicit `super()`, and the chain continues upward until it reaches `Object`. For example, if you write `class SavingsAccount extends Account {}` with no constructor, the compiler creates `SavingsAccount() { super(); }` behind the scenes.

Constructor chaining with `this(...)` lets you provide convenient overloaded constructors while keeping all the real initialization and validation in one primary constructor. For instance, a two-argument constructor can call `this(accountId, holderName, BigDecimal.ZERO)` to delegate to a three-argument primary constructor, so there is a single source of truth for the setup logic and no duplicated validation. A delegating constructor that uses `this(...)` does not itself call `super(...)`; the constructor it eventually delegates to is the one responsible for the super call.

The no-executable-code-before rule is strict. You cannot compute a value and then call `super(...)`; the call must be literally first. You can, however, pass expressions as arguments, including calls to static methods, because evaluating the arguments is considered part of making the call. For example `super(validateId(id), holderName)` is legal because `validateId(id)` is just computing an argument, whereas assigning a field before `super(...)` is not.

The compile-error case follows directly from the implicit-super rule. The implicit no-argument `super()` requires the superclass to have an accessible no-argument constructor. But the moment a class declares any constructor, the compiler stops generating a default one, so a base class that declares only constructors with arguments has no no-argument constructor at all. In that situation the implicit `super()` cannot be satisfied, and every subclass constructor must explicitly call an available `super(args)` as its first statement, or the subclass will not compile. This is often exactly what you want, because it forces every subclass to supply the mandatory information the base class needs. The senior-level nuance is that this behaviour is a feature, not an annoyance: by deliberately omitting a no-arg constructor in a base class like `Account`, you make it impossible to create a half-initialized account, and the compiler enforces that discipline on every subclass.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India our customers are Rajesh, a software engineer with savings account SAV2001 holding ten lakh rupees, and Priya, a property owner with current account CUR3001 holding two lakh fifty thousand rupees.

Problem 1 — our base `Account` class needs three mandatory pieces of information to exist at all: an account id, a holder name, and an opening balance. We deliberately do not want anyone to create an account without these, because a half-built account with a null id once caused a reconciliation nightmare. We want to show that by giving `Account` only an argument-taking constructor, the compiler forces every subclass to pass those mandatory values up with an explicit `super(args)`, making a half-initialized account impossible.

Problem 2 — our `SavingsAccount` subclass is created in several ways: sometimes with a specified interest rate, and sometimes with a default interest rate. We do not want to duplicate the balance and id validation in every overload. We want to show constructor chaining, where a convenience constructor delegates through `this(...)` to one primary constructor that does all the validation and makes the single `super(args)` call, so there is exactly one place where the real setup lives.

Our runnable demo will define a base `Account` with only a three-argument constructor and debit and credit methods, a `SavingsAccount` subclass with a primary four-argument constructor that calls `super(args)` and a convenience three-argument constructor that delegates via `this(...)`, and a `main` that creates Rajesh's savings account both ways, performs a transfer to Priya, and logs the construction order so the top-down initialization is visible.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's savings account (SAV2001, 1000000) built the convenience way, Priya's account (CUR3001, 250000, rate 0.035) built the primary way, and a rent amount of 50000.

Step 1 — Rajesh's account is created with the three-argument convenience constructor. Its first statement is `this(...)`, which delegates to the four-argument primary constructor, passing a default interest rate of 0.04. No super call happens yet in the convenience constructor itself.

Step 2 — inside the primary constructor, the first statement is `super(accountId, holderName, balance)`. The base `Account` constructor runs first, validating the id and balance and initializing the base fields. The log shows the base part initialized before the savings part, proving top-down construction.

Step 3 — after `super(...)` returns, the primary constructor validates and sets the interest rate, completing Rajesh's object. He now has a fully built savings account with the default 4 percent rate.

Step 4 — Priya's account is created directly with the four-argument primary constructor and an explicit rate of 0.035. Its `super(...)` runs first to build the base part, then the rate is set. No delegation is involved this time.

Step 5 — the transfer runs. Rajesh is debited 50000 to 950000 and Priya is credited 50000 to 300000, and the success is logged. Throughout, the compiler guaranteed that no account could ever be created without its mandatory id, holder, and balance, because `Account` has no no-arg constructor.

Final output:

```text
2026-10-30 19:31:22 INFO    Rajesh account created, default rate=0.04
2026-10-30 19:31:22 INFO    Priya account created, rate=0.035
2026-10-30 19:31:22 INFO    Transfer 50000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001 SUCCESS
2026-10-30 19:31:22 INFO    Rajesh=950000 Priya=300000
```


sections.s6_takeaway:
Within a constructor, this with arguments delegates to another constructor of the same class, and super with arguments invokes a constructor of the direct superclass. Whichever of these you use must be the very first statement of the constructor, and because they both compete for that single first slot, a constructor can contain at most one of them and never both, and no executable code may run before it. The reason is that the language guarantees the superclass part of the object is fully initialized before any subclass code runs, which this top-down ordering makes possible.

If a constructor contains neither a this nor a super call, the compiler implicitly inserts a no-argument super as the first statement. That is why a class with no explicit constructor still initializes its parent correctly, because the default constructor the compiler generates contains that implicit super, and every constructor ultimately chains all the way up to Object. Constructor chaining with this is how I provide convenient overloaded constructors while keeping all the real initialization and validation in a single primary constructor, so there is one source of truth and no duplicated checks. A delegating constructor does not call super itself; the constructor it eventually delegates to is responsible for the super call.

The compile-error case follows straight from the implicit-super rule. The implicit no-argument super needs the superclass to have an accessible no-argument constructor, but the moment a class declares any constructor the compiler stops generating a default one. So a base class that declares only constructors with arguments has no no-argument constructor, the implicit super cannot be satisfied, and every subclass constructor must explicitly call an available super with arguments as its first statement, or it fails to compile. I treat this as a feature rather than a nuisance.

In our account model at National Bank of India the base Account class needs an account id, a holder name, and an opening balance to exist at all, so I deliberately gave it only an argument-taking constructor and no no-arg constructor. The payoff is that the compiler makes it impossible to create a half-built account with a null id, which had once caused us a reconciliation nightmare, because every subclass is forced to pass those mandatory values up with an explicit super call. For the SavingsAccount subclass I funnel a convenience constructor that takes a default interest rate through this delegation into one primary four-argument constructor that performs all the validation and makes the single super call, so there is exactly one place the setup logic lives. And because super always runs before the subclass body, the inherited account fields are guaranteed to be set before the savings-specific interest rate is assigned, giving clean, predictable top-down initialization every time.

---

keyPoints: this() and super() must be the first statement — at most one
super() is auto-inserted if you write neither this() nor super()
Constructor chaining: this(a) calls this(a,b) calls super(a,b,c)
Circular this() calls cause compile error — must eventually call super()
